Kumar Manglam Pandey Ziqi Zhou Elio Al Alam Sebastian Santoni Perez De Obanos

This post walks through a complete fairness and bias audit of machine learning models for PTSD prediction, using the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2022 — a nationally representative dataset of 67,079 Canadians.

If you've ever wondered how to actually do fairness-aware machine learning — not just the theory, but the full pipeline including the bugs, the fixes, the charts, and the production-ready code — this is the post for you.

By the end, you'll know how to:

  • Set up a fairness-preserving preprocessing pipeline
  • Compute EOD, DPD, and Equalized Odds
  • Use bootstrap confidence intervals for group-level metrics
  • Apply SMOTE correctly (including the double-compensation trap)
  • Run intersectional fairness analysis
  • Interpret results in clinical context — not just as numbers
📋 Context This project was built for a graduate course on Fairness and Bias in AI. The four-person team split responsibilities: Sebastian (preprocessing), Manglam (Decision Tree models), Elio (MLP/neural nets), and Ziqi (debiasing + visualisation). The code is designed as sequential Jupyter cells — each team member's section pastes after the previous one.

1 Why Fairness in Mental Health AI?

PTSD affects roughly 9% of Canadians at some point in their lives — but it's severely underdiagnosed, and the gap is worst for the people who need care most. Indigenous communities face PTSD rates 2–3× the national average. Immigrants carry pre-migration trauma. People with disabilities face compounding barriers to both diagnosis and treatment.

Now imagine training an AI model to screen for PTSD and deploying it without a fairness audit. The model learns from historical data — which encodes all of those existing disparities. A model with 94.4% overall accuracy can still miss 80% of PTSD cases in a minority group, because the dominant class (no PTSD) is 95.6% of the dataset.

🔑 The core tension Optimising for overall accuracy in an imbalanced dataset is the same as optimising for the majority class. This is not just a technical problem — it's an equity problem. Communities already underserved by the healthcare system get the worst model performance.

This is why a proper fairness audit isn't optional — it's the minimum bar for responsible deployment of any clinical ML tool.

2 The Dataset: CCHS 2022

The Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2022 is a cross-sectional probability sample of 67,079 Canadians aged 12 and older. It's one of the most comprehensive public health datasets available in Canada, covering physical health, mental health, socioeconomic status, and healthcare access.

Key Numbers

StatValueNotes
Raw respondents67,079After quality checks
Usable rows (per run)~59,000After preprocessing per target/attr pair
Original features255Before engineering
Final features~68After engineering + exclusions
PTSD positive rate4.44%Severe class imbalance
Train / Test split80 / 20Stratified on target
⚠️ The class imbalance problem 4.44% positive rate means a model that predicts "no PTSD" for everyone achieves 95.56% accuracy. This is why accuracy is a terrible metric here. We use Recall (sensitivity) as our primary performance metric — for a screening tool, missing a true case (false negative) is the costliest error.

3 Sensitive Attributes

We evaluate eight sensitive attributes. Critically: none of these are used as model inputs. They're excluded from the feature matrix and used for post-hoc fairness evaluation only. Using them as inputs would constitute direct discrimination.

4 The Preprocessing Pipeline

Sebastian's preprocessing function is the foundation everything else builds on. The key architectural decision: preprocess_df() always operates on a copy of the original dataframe, and each (target, sensitive_attribute) pair gets its own independent preprocessing run. This prevents data leakage across runs.

1

Drop not-stated + NaN

Remove rows where the target or sensitive attribute equals the coded "not stated" value (9 for most variables, 99 for continuous ones). Then call dropna() on those two columns — critical for is_immigrant and is_disabled which carry genuine NaN from valid-skip handling.

2

Impute all other columns

Binary and categorical features → mode. Ordinal features → rounded median. Targets are NEVER imputed — only dropped when "not stated".

3

Recode target

CCHS encodes Yes/No as 1/2. We recode to 1/0. This happens after preprocessing returns — never inside it. This distinction matters because imputation runs on the raw coding.

4

Build feature matrix

Exclude ALL target columns + the current sensitive attribute. One-hot encode non-ordinal categoricals. Impute residual NaN using training set medians only — no test-set leakage.

5

Stratified 80/20 split

Split on the target column to preserve the 4.44% positive rate in both train and test sets.

Core Preprocessing Code

def preprocess_df(df, target, sensitive_attribute):
    """
    Returns a cleaned copy of df for one (target, attr) pair.
    NEVER modifies the original dataframe.
    
    KEY FIX: dropna() after drop_not_stated() eliminates
    ghost NaN groups that survive the code-9 check.
    """
    df_new = df.copy()

    # Drop coded "not stated" (9 or 99)
    df_new = drop_not_stated(df_new, target)
    df_new = drop_not_stated(df_new, sensitive_attribute)

    # ── CRITICAL FIX ─────────────────────────────────────
    # is_immigrant and is_disabled contain genuine pandas NaN
    # from valid-skip handling. NaN != 9 is True in pandas,
    # so those rows SURVIVE drop_not_stated() and appear as
    # ghost "nan" groups (n=0) in all output CSVs.
    # ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    df_new = df_new.dropna(subset=[sensitive_attribute, target])

    # Impute all OTHER columns (never the focal ones)
    other_targets = [t for t in targets if t != target]
    other_attrs   = [a for a in all_sensitive_attributes
                     if a != sensitive_attribute]

    for col in other_targets + other_attrs:
        if col not in df_new.columns:   # guard for dropped cols
            continue
        df_new = impute_missing(df_new, col)

    return df_new


def impute_missing(df, col):
    ns_val = 99 if col in ordinal_cols_99 else 9
    if col in (targets + binary_cols + non_ordinal_cols):
        val = df[col][df[col] != ns_val].mode()[0]
    else:
        val = round(df[col][df[col] != ns_val].median())
    df[col] = df[col].replace(ns_val, val)
    return df

5 Models: DT and MLP

Decision Tree (DT)

scikit-learn DecisionTreeClassifier with class_weight='balanced' as the interpretable baseline. Hyperparameters are tuned via out-of-bag bootstrap (see Section 7). All 8 sensitive attribute runs converged to max_depth=5, suggesting a relatively shallow decision boundary for PTSD.

def bootstrap_tune(X_train, y_train, param_grid, n_bootstrap=30):
    """
    Select best DT hyperparameters using OOB F1.
    ~37% of rows are left out per bootstrap iteration
    → unbiased F1 estimate without touching the test set.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    n = len(X_train)
    best_f1, best_params = 0, {}

    for params in param_grid:
        scores = []
        for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
            boot_idx = rng.choice(n, size=n, replace=True)
            oob_idx  = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), boot_idx)
            if len(oob_idx) == 0: continue

            dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(**params,
                     class_weight="balanced", random_state=42)
            dt.fit(X_train[boot_idx], y_train[boot_idx])
            scores.append(f1_score(
                y_train[oob_idx], dt.predict(X_train[oob_idx]),
                zero_division=0))

        mean_f1 = np.mean(scores) if scores else 0
        if mean_f1 > best_f1:
            best_f1, best_params = mean_f1, params

    return best_params

Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)

3-layer MLP with BatchNorm and Dropout. EarlyStopping on validation AUC. Threshold set to 0.3 instead of 0.5 — deliberately lower because in a screening context, maximising recall at the cost of some precision is the clinically correct tradeoff.

def build_mlp(input_dim, lr=1e-3):
    model = keras.Sequential([
        layers.Input(shape=(input_dim,)),
        layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
        layers.BatchNormalization(),
        layers.Dropout(0.3),
        layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
        layers.BatchNormalization(),
        layers.Dropout(0.3),
        layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
        layers.BatchNormalization(),
        layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"),
    ])
    model.compile(
        optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(lr),
        loss="binary_crossentropy",
        metrics=["auc", "precision", "recall"],
    )
    return model

6 Fairness Metrics Explained

We implement three fairness metrics manually (no external libraries like AIF360 — this matters because it forces you to understand what you're computing).

EOD
Equal Opportunity Difference
max(TPR_g) − min(TPR_g)

Primary metric. Measures recall inequality across groups. EOD = 0 means every group has equal true positive rate. For PTSD screening, a missed diagnosis is the costliest error.

DPD
Demographic Parity Difference
max(pred_rate_g) − min(pred_rate_g)

Context-sensitive. Measures prediction rate inequality. High DPD can reflect genuine prevalence differences, not just model error — so interpret carefully.

EqOdd
Equalized Odds
max(TPR_gap, FPR_gap)

Stricter than EOD. When EqOdd substantially exceeds EOD, the FPR gap dominates — the model over-predicts for truly-negative members of certain groups.

def compute_fairness_exact(y_true, y_pred, groups):
    tprs, fprs, pred_rates = [], [], []

    for g in sorted(groups.dropna().unique()):
        mask   = groups.values == g
        yt, yp = y_true[mask], y_pred[mask]
        n_pos  = yt.sum()
        n_neg  = (1 - yt).sum()

        tpr = float(yp[yt == 1].mean()) if n_pos > 0 else np.nan
        fpr = float(yp[yt == 0].mean()) if n_neg > 0 else np.nan
        pred_rates.append(float(yp.mean()))

        if not np.isnan(tpr): tprs.append(tpr)
        if not np.isnan(fpr): fprs.append(fpr)

    eod   = max(tprs) - min(tprs) if len(tprs) >= 2 else np.nan
    dpd   = max(pred_rates) - min(pred_rates)
    tpr_g = (max(tprs) - min(tprs)) if len(tprs) >= 2 else 0.0
    fpr_g = (max(fprs) - min(fprs)) if len(fprs) >= 2 else 0.0

    return {"eod": round(eod, 4),
            "dpd": round(dpd, 4),
            "eqodd": round(max(tpr_g, fpr_g), 4)}

7 Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

We use bootstrap in two completely different ways — and confusing them is a common mistake:

PassApplied ToN IterationsPurpose
bootstrap_tune() Training set (OOB) 30 Select DT hyperparameters. ~37% of rows left out per iteration ((1-1/n)^n → 1/e ≈ 0.368). Unbiased F1 without touching test set.
bootstrap_evaluate() Test set (resampled) 200 Compute 95% CI for all metrics. Resamples test set with replacement 200×, computes 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
🔑 Critical implementation detail: key dtype mismatch The most insidious bug we found: group_ci keys were stored as the original Python dtype (int 0, float 0.0). But evaluate_groups() stores the "group" column as str(g). So _gci.get("0") returned {} when the key was 0 (int) — silently setting ALL CI columns to NaN.

Fix: group_ci = {str(g): summarise(recs) for g, recs in group_records.items()} 
def bootstrap_evaluate(model, X_test, y_test, test_groups,
                         n_bootstrap=200, ci_level=95, seed=42):
    rng    = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n      = len(y_test)
    lo_pct = (100 - ci_level) / 2   # 2.5
    hi_pct = 100 - lo_pct             # 97.5

    group_records = {}

    for _ in range(n_bootstrap):
        idx      = rng.choice(n, size=n, replace=True)
        X_b      = X_test[idx]
        y_b      = y_test[idx]
        groups_b = test_groups.iloc[idx].reset_index(drop=True)

        if len(np.unique(y_b)) < 2: continue

        y_pred = model.predict(X_b)
        y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_b)[:, 1]

        for g in groups_b.unique():
            mask = groups_b.values == g
            yg, yp = y_b[mask], y_pred[mask]
            if mask.sum() < 5: continue

            group_records.setdefault(g, []).append({
                "recall"   : recall_score(yg, yp, zero_division=0),
                "f1"       : f1_score(yg, yp, zero_division=0),
                "precision": precision_score(yg, yp, zero_division=0),
            })

    def summarise(records):
        return {k: (
            round(float(np.nanmean([r[k] for r in records])), 4),
            round(float(np.nanstd([r[k] for r in records])), 4),
            round(float(np.nanpercentile([r[k] for r in records], lo_pct)), 4),
            round(float(np.nanpercentile([r[k] for r in records], hi_pct)), 4),
        ) for k in records[0].keys()}

    # ── CRITICAL: str(g) keys to match evaluate_groups() output ──
    return {str(g): summarise(recs)
            for g, recs in group_records.items() if recs}

9 Intersectional Analysis

This is where things get really interesting — and where per-axis audits fall dangerously short.

We evaluated the intersection of sex × is_indigenous. Per-axis EOD is: sex = 0.072, is_indigenous = 0.050. But at the intersection:

Intersectional EOD = Female×Indigenous recall (0.846) − Male×Non-Indigenous recall (0.634) = 0.212

That's 3× the per-axis sex EOD and 4.2× the per-axis is_indigenous EOD. If you only run per-axis audits, you miss this entirely.

Intersection GroupNPositivesRecallF1Interpretation
Female × Non-Indigenous6,5073430.6970.221Largest group; moderate performance
Female × Indigenous151260.8460.436Highest F1; model detects PTSD well here
Male × Non-Indigenous5,4341640.6340.148Most missed PTSD cases by count
Male × Indigenous10590.6670.2559 positives — CI width > 0.6, very unstable

Figure 4: F1 heatmap for sex × is_indigenous intersection. Rows = method, columns = intersection cells. The 0×1 cell (Female × Indigenous) consistently has highest F1.

⚠️ Lesson for practitioners Always run intersectional analysis. Per-axis EOD of 0.072 and 0.050 sounds fine. Intersectional EOD of 0.212 is unacceptable for a clinical tool. The two numbers describe completely different realities.

10 Debiasing: SMOTE vs Threshold Optimisation

Method 1: SMOTE (Chosen)

SMOTE generates synthetic positive-class training samples by interpolating in feature space between existing minority instances and their k-nearest neighbours.

🔑 The double-compensation trap If you use class_weight='balanced' AND SMOTE at the same time, you're correcting for class imbalance twice. This degrades both F1 and fairness. When using SMOTE, set class_weight=None. 
from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE

def run_dt_smote(target, sensitive_attr, baseline_res):
    X_train = baseline_res["_X_train"]
    y_train = baseline_res["_y_train"]

    n_min = int(y_train.sum())
    k_nn  = max(1, min(5, n_min - 1))  # cap k for tiny groups

    sm = SMOTE(random_state=42, k_neighbors=k_nn)
    X_res, y_res = sm.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)

    # class_weight=None — SMOTE handles imbalance.
    # 'balanced' on top double-compensates and hurts F1+fairness.
    dt = DecisionTreeClassifier(
        **baseline_res["best_params"],
        class_weight=None,
        random_state=42
    )
    dt.fit(X_res, y_res)
    return dt

Method 2: Threshold Optimisation (Reference Only — Why It Fails)

Find the optimal decision threshold per group on the validation set. Sounds great in theory. Fails catastrophically in practice for small groups.

🚫 Why threshold optimisation fails for small groups is_indigenous has only 12 validation-set positives. The 95% CI on any threshold-sensitive metric spans 0.15–0.30 — meaning the "optimal" threshold is just noise. When we ran it: is_indigenous EOD went from 0.050 → 0.104 (it got worse). Our recommendation: only use threshold optimisation when you have at least 50 validation-set positives per group.

✅ SMOTE (Use this)

  • Reduces EOD on 5 of 8 DT attributes
  • Numerically stable across group sizes
  • Pre-processing — works before training
  • No per-group validation set needed
  • Model-agnostic (works with DT, MLP, XGBoost)
  • class_weight=None to avoid double-compensation

❌ Threshold Optimisation (Avoid for small groups)

  • Fails for groups with < 50 val-set positives
  • Worsened is_indigenous EOD by 109%
  • Creates false precision (thresholds to 3 dp)
  • Requires separate validation set per group
  • Post-processing — can't fix representation gaps
  • Instability compounds across groups

ℹ️ Why SMOTE fails for is_indigenous SMOTE generates synthetic samples by interpolating in feature space between existing minority instances. But is_indigenous is strongly correlated with household_food_security_status and income_quintile. SMOTE generates synthetic samples that are statistically similar to the existing ones in that correlated feature space — so the model's learned boundary doesn't substantially change. This is a fundamental limitation: SMOTE operates in observable feature space, not in the causal space of structural disadvantage.

12 The Bugs We Hit (and How We Fixed Them)

This section is gold for practitioners. Every one of these bugs took real debugging time to diagnose.

Bug #1 All CI columns are NaN — silently
Root Cause

bootstrap_evaluate() stored group_ci keys as their original Python dtype — 0 (int), 0.0 (float). But evaluate_groups() stores group as str(g). So _gci.get("0", {}) found nothing when the key was integer 0.

✓ Fix 
# Old (broken)
group_ci = {g: summarise(recs) for g, recs in group_records.items()}

# Fixed — normalize keys to str()
group_ci = {str(g): summarise(recs)
            for g, recs in group_records.items()}
Bug #2 NaN ghost groups in is_immigrant and is_disabled
Root Cause

drop_not_stated() removes rows where col == 9. But binary columns can also hold genuine pandas NaN from valid-skip handling. In pandas, NaN != 9 evaluates to True, so NaN rows survived and appeared as a "nan" group with n=0 in all CSVs.

✓ Fix 
df_new = drop_not_stated(df_new, target)
df_new = drop_not_stated(df_new, sensitive_attribute)
# ── Add this line ──────────────────────────────────────
df_new = df_new.dropna(subset=[sensitive_attribute, target])
Bug #3 KeyError: 'health_region'
Root Cause

preprocess_df() loops over all_sensitive_attributes to impute them. 'health_region' (renamed RHC_05) was dropped during feature engineering. The imputation loop hit it and raised KeyError.

✓ Fix 
for col in other_targets + other_attributes:
    if col not in df_new.columns:  # ← add this guard
        continue
    df_new = impute_missing(df_new, col)
Bug #4 ValueError: The truth value of a DataFrame is ambiguous
Root Cause

Used Python's or operator to select between two dict lookups that return DataFrames. pandas overrides __bool__ to raise instead of returning True/False.

✓ Fix 
# Old (broken) — bool(DataFrame) raises
_test_df = (_base_res.get("_test_df") or _base_res.get("test_df"))

# Fixed — use key existence check
_test_df = (_base_res["_test_df"] if "_test_df" in _base_res
            else _base_res["test_df"])
Bug #5 ValueError: cannot insert target, already exists
Root Cause

Code called df.insert() twice for the "target" column — first to insert it at position 0, then again inside a loop. df.insert() doesn't overwrite by default.

✓ Fix 
# Use direct assignment instead of insert()
_g["target"]     = _t
_g["method"]     = "mlp_baseline"
_g["model_type"] = "mlp"

# Then reorder explicitly
front = ["target", "sensitive_attr", "method", "model_type"]
_g = _g[front + [c for c in _g.columns if c not in front]]

13 Key Findings

Figure 10: 95% CI forest plot for age_group. Group 1 (18–24y, only 9 test positives) shows CI widths > 0.6 — reporting only the point estimate for this group would be methodologically indefensible.

Figure 11: 95% CI for is_indigenous. DT+SMOTE has a similar point estimate to DT Tuned (0.593 vs 0.596) but significantly wider CI [0.493, 0.688] vs [0.549, 0.630].

F1

Tuning reliably worsens fairness

Bootstrap-tuned DT improved recall by 30–50 percentage points but increased EOD on 7 of 8 attributes (worst: is_disabled ↑208%, is_immigrant ↑300%). There is no free lunch. Fairness interventions are mandatory, not optional.

F2

DPD ≠ EOD — distinguish carefully

is_indigenous shows DPD = 0.239 but EOD = 0.050 (MLP Baseline). High DPD reflects genuine prevalence differences — Indigenous populations experience PTSD at 2–3× the national rate. A model that achieves DPD parity by predicting PTSD less for Indigenous respondents would be more harmful, not fairer.

F3

Intersectional disparities are multiplicative

Per-axis EOD: sex = 0.072, is_indigenous = 0.050. Intersectional EOD (Female×Indigenous vs Male×Non-Indigenous) = 0.212 — 3× larger. A fairness audit using only per-axis metrics severely understates actual harm.

F4

SMOTE reduces EOD on 5/8 DT attributes

Largest reductions: is_immigrant −65%, sex −53%, age_group −52%. SMOTE failed for is_indigenous (+109%) because the sensitive attribute is strongly correlated with socioeconomic proxy features — synthetic samples don't change the model's learned boundary for this group.

F5

Higher capacity model ≠ fairer model

MLP recall (87–91%) far exceeds DT Tuned (65–70%). But MLP EOD for age_group (0.261) nearly matches DT Tuned (0.324). Raw model power doesn't solve structural data bias.

F6

95% CI is non-negotiable for health equity ML

age_group group 1 (18–24y, 9 test positives): recall CI = [0.167, 0.778] — a width of 0.611. Reporting only the point estimate for this group would be misleading. Wide CI = low confidence, not low recall.

14 Recommendations for Practitioners

Checklist for a Production Fairness Audit

✓

Report EOD with 95% CI for every sensitive attribute

Never report point estimates alone. Groups with fewer than 30 test-set positives should be flagged with wide-CI warnings.

✓

Exclude sensitive attributes from feature matrices

Evaluate them post-hoc only. Include them as features = direct discrimination. Their correlation with other features means proxy discrimination can still occur, but that's a separate problem to address with feature selection.

✓

Run intersectional analysis for all high-prevalence pairings

At minimum: sex × each other attribute. Per-axis audits understate intersectional harm by 3× in our data.

✓

Apply SMOTE with class_weight=None

Not class_weight='balanced'. Not both. SMOTE handles class imbalance; adding balanced weight on top double-compensates and degrades both F1 and fairness.

✓

Interpret DPD in epidemiological context

High DPD can mean genuine prevalence differences, not just model error. Before concluding a model is biased because of high DPD, check whether the groups actually have different outcome prevalence rates in ground-truth data.

✓

Set minimum group size guards for threshold optimisation

Use threshold optimisation only when groups have ≥50 validation-set positives. Below that, the chosen threshold is noise and EOD reliably worsens.

This work was completed as part of EECS 6320: Fairness and Bias in Artificial Intelligence at York University (March 2026). The full codebase can be accessed here.

Data: Statistics Canada, Canadian Community Health Survey 2022 (Cat. No. 82-625-X). All fairness metrics computed manually without external fairness libraries.
